title: Switzerland holds at zero through a higher energy-inflation peak
summary: The Swiss National Bank kept its policy rate at 0% on 24 September. It judged that a higher near-term inflation peak could coexist with price stability over its forecast horizon and with a monetary stance that supported activity. Oil products had been dearer than expected, while a weaker franc contributed to a smaller upward revision further out. Both the September forecast and its June predecessor assumed a policy rate of zero throughout. Their divergence therefore shows how the SNB’s assessment of the outlook changed under the same interest-rate assumption. It does not establish what investors expected the bank to do at subsequent meetings. The bank also retained the option of acting in the foreign exchange market if monetary conditions required it. (Decision, p. 1; forecast chart, p. 3.)

Observed inflation rose from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August. Goods prices were higher than a year earlier for the first time since May 2024, principally owing to oil products. The bank expected inflation to rise further in the fourth quarter, then recede during 2027 as energy inflation abated. The quarterly table makes the timing clearer than the annual averages alone. In June the bank had projected 0.8% inflation in both the final quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. September’s forecast put both quarters at 1.2%. By the second half of 2027 it projected 0.7% in each quarter. The projected inflation rate then rose gradually. For 2026, 2027 and 2028, the September annual averages were 0.7%, 0.8% and 0.8% respectively, against June projections of 0.6%, 0.6% and 0.7%. The chart compares year-on-year CPI growth, so the forecast decline during 2027 describes slower price increases. (Inflation assessment, p. 1; chart and tables, p. 3.)

It is possible to date the forecast surprise fairly precisely. The second quarter of 2026, forecast at 0.6% in June, subsequently recorded 0.6%. Both forecast vintages also put the third quarter at 0.7%. Their paths then diverged by 0.4 percentage point in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first two quarters of 2027, before the gap narrowed to 0.1 point in the second half of 2027. Higher prices for oil products therefore changed the expected timing and height of the inflation peak much more than the starting observation. Farther out, some extra pressure remained, partly reflecting the franc’s depreciation. The figures are rounded year-on-year rates for individual quarters. A market-based inflation rate over a calendar year would have a different exposure to that short-lived bulge (observed inflation table and conditional forecast table, p. 3).

The activity figures gave the bank reasons both for confidence and for caution. Second-quarter Swiss GDP had risen exceptionally strongly, with an unusually large contribution from chemicals and pharmaceuticals. The SNB judged that underlying momentum was weaker than the headline suggested, even though growth across the rest of the economy had been solid and broadly based. Capacity utilisation was below average, especially in manufacturing, and unemployment had edged higher into early summer. The bank anticipated moderate growth in the following quarters, supported by overseas demand, domestic monetary conditions and the franc’s recent depreciation. It expected full-year growth of 1.5–2% in 2026 and maintained its projection of about 1.5% for 2027. (Domestic outlook, p. 2.)

The weaker franc worked on both sides of the forecast. The bank identified it as one reason for stronger medium-term inflation and as a source of support for Swiss output, alongside foreign demand and domestic monetary policy. Those two statements can hold at the same time if exchange-rate changes affect both import costs and exporters’ competitiveness. The release describes the direction of these effects but gives no separate exchange-rate elasticity. It also keeps the terms for reserve balances distinct from currency policy. Eligible sight deposits earn 0% up to the threshold, while the 0.25-percentage-point discount implies a rate of −0.25% on balances above it. Holding the policy rate at zero therefore did not mean every franc of reserves earned zero (decision and inflation assessment, p. 1, and growth outlook, p. 2).

The main threat to that combination came from abroad. Second-quarter global growth had exceeded expectations, yet the bank envisaged only moderate growth ahead and persistent inflation pressure in many economies. It noted that interest rates had risen in both the euro area and the United States. A worsening conflict in the Middle East could drive energy prices materially above the baseline, lifting inflation while weakening global demand. Trade policy and the exchange rate added uncertainty. For portfolios exposed to Swiss rates and the franc, a pertinent inference is that the policy significance of a rise in headline inflation depends on both its duration and the accompanying change in demand. The assessment gives no threshold for an intervention or policy-rate adjustment. (Decision, p. 1; international outlook and risk discussion, p. 2.)

questions.question: How much of the inflation revision would survive a reversal in oil prices?
questions.detail: The bank separates an energy-led near-term revision from a smaller medium-term change partly attributed to the franc. It does not quantify these contributions separately. That distinction matters to the sensitivity of Swiss front-end rates after an energy-price surprise. Compare official Swiss CPI components, import prices and contemporaneous exchange rates with the forecast assumptions; examine SNB technical material on exchange-rate pass-through for the expected lags.

questions.question: How much external-demand weakness could accompany another energy shock?
questions.detail: The SNB identifies a joint inflation and growth risk but gives no alternative numerical path. Manufacturing capacity was already underused despite strong headline GDP. A meaningful external slowdown could change the relative exposures of Swiss rates and cyclical equities. Consult the Swiss national accounts and capacity surveys, separating chemicals and pharmaceuticals from other industries, and compare exporters’ new orders with movements in energy costs.

questions.question: What policy and currency outcomes were already reflected in market prices?
questions.detail: The document establishes the bank’s constant-rate forecasting assumption and its willingness to intervene. It gives no evidence of actual September intervention or of the rate path priced by investors. For implementation, retrieve contemporaneous Swiss overnight-indexed-swap quotes and franc option prices. Compare their pre-decision and post-decision levels with the information in this assessment before treating the zero-rate assumption as a market signal.
